business.what_it_does: Tally is a form builder that works like a document — you type questions directly on the page and insert blocks (contact info, payments, signatures, file uploads, ratings, etc.) the way you would in Notion, with no coding required.

entries.claim: A file upload form lets respondents send files directly without needing to sign up.
entries.verbatim: A file upload form lets you collect files directly from respondents, without the need for them to sign up.

entries.claim: File upload forms are free on all Tally plans, with no limit on the number of files you can collect.
entries.verbatim: File upload forms are free on all Tally plans, with no limit on the number of files you can collect.

entries.claim: The free Tally plan supports individual files up to 10 MB.
entries.verbatim: The free plan supports individual files up to 10 MB.

entries.claim: Tally lets you add a file upload field to any form and start collecting images, PDFs, videos, audio files, and documents in minutes.
entries.verbatim: With Tally, you can add a file upload field to any form and start collecting images, PDFs, videos, audio files, and documents in minutes.

entries.claim: Unlike Google Forms and other tools, Tally respondents don't need to log in to upload files.
entries.verbatim: Unlike Google Forms and other tools, your respondents don’t need to log in to upload files.

entries.claim: Respondents can upload multiple files, with configurable minimum and maximum number of file uploads.
entries.verbatim: If you want respondents to be able to upload multiple files, enable the `Multiple files`option. This will allow you to define the desired `minimum`and `maximum`number of file uploads.

entries.claim: Form builders can enable a Max file size setting so respondents see the file size limit in the upload block.
entries.verbatim: Enable `Max file size` to set a file size limit. Respondents will see the maximum file size limit in the file upload block.

entries.claim: Form builders can restrict uploads to specific allowed file types, such as all image files or just .jpg files.
entries.verbatim: To only accept certain file types, enable `Allowed files` and select the file type(s) you want to accept. For example: - If you only want to accept image files, regardless of the type, select `All image files` - If you only want to accept .jpg files, select `.jpg`

entries.claim: Conditional logic can show or hide the file upload block based on a respondent's previous answers.
entries.verbatim: You can use [conditional logic](https://www.notion.so/6ea9699f446740c8937058ef0dc4dea1) to show or hide the file upload block depending on a respondent's previous answers.

entries.claim: Viewing uploaded files in the Submissions tab requires being logged in to your Tally account.
entries.verbatim: You need to be logged in to your Tally account to view them.

entries.claim: A 'Download file uploads' button lets you batch download all files from a submissions page at once.
entries.verbatim: Use the 'Download file uploads' button at the top of the submissions page to download all files at once.

entries.claim: When exporting file uploads to third-party tools like Google Sheets, an access token is added to the links so files are accessible without being logged into Tally.
entries.verbatim: When you export your file uploads to third-party tools using our integrations, an access token is added to the links, which makes them accessible without the need to be logged in. For example, if you export form submissions to a Google Sheet, anyone with access to that Sheet can click the file upload URL and access the file (without being logged into Tally).

entries.claim: There is no limit to the number of files you can upload or the total storage used.
entries.verbatim: No, there's no limit to the number of files you can upload or the total storage.

entries.claim: Uploaded files are preserved with no time limit as long as the account is open and responses aren't deleted.
entries.verbatim: No, there's no time limit. As long as your account is open and the responses are not deleted from your account, the files are preserved.

entries.verbatim: Webhooks are available **for free** to all Tally users.

entries.claim: When a Tally form is submitted, a notification containing the response data is sent to the configured URL in JSON format via a POST request.
entries.verbatim: When someone submits a Tally form, a notification containing the response data gets sent to your URL in **JSON** format via a **POST** request.

entries.claim: Tally webhook endpoints have a 10-second timeout to process and respond to a new submission.
entries.verbatim: A webhook endpoint has a **10-second timeout** to process and respond to a new submission. If the processing takes longer, it's advisable to call another service internally.

entries.claim: Tally webhook requests can include a Tally-Signature header containing a SHA256 cryptographic hash of the payload for verification.
entries.verbatim: When this option is enabled, the webhook requests will contain a `Tally-Signature` header. The value of this header is a SHA256 cryptographic hash of the webhook payload.

entries.claim: Tally supports connecting unlimited webhook URLs, which can be paused via a toggle.
entries.verbatim: You can connect unlimited webhook URLs and pause them by clicking the toggle.

entries.claim: If a webhook delivery fails, Tally retries after 5 minutes, then 30 minutes, then 1 hour, then 6 hours, then 1 day.
entries.verbatim: 1. The first retry occurs after 5 minutes 2. If the first retry fails, the second retry is scheduled after 30 minutes 3. If the second retry fails, the third retry is scheduled after 1 hour 4. If the third retry fails, the fourth retry is scheduled after 6 hours 5. If the fourth retry fails, the fifth retry is scheduled after 1 day

entries.claim: If all retries fail, Tally sends a one-time email to the form owner and creator with the reason and a link to fix it.
entries.verbatim: If all retries fail, we'll also send a one-time email to the form owner and creator with the reason and a link to fix it. We won't email again for the same failure until it resolves and happens again.

entries.claim: Webhooks created via an integration can only be removed from within that integration.
entries.verbatim: If the webhook is created from an [integration](https://tally.so/help/integrations), then you can only remove the webhook in the integration where you originally created it.

entries.claim: Tally offers integrations with Zapier, Make, Pipedream, and Integrately for syncing form submissions.
entries.verbatim: If you're instead looking for a non-technical way to sync Tally form submissions with other apps, check out our [Zapier](/help/zapier-integration), [Make](/help/make-integration), [Pipedream](/help/pipedream-integration) or [Integrately](/help/integrately-integration) integrations.

segments.name: A freelance designer or one-person studio who spends the first two weeks of every project chasing brand assets out of a client's inbox
segments.situation: Every new engagement starts the same way: they need the logo in a usable format, the old brand guidelines PDF, photography the client owns, a rough brief, the billing details and whoever's sign-off they'll need later. None of it arrives in one place. It comes back as a reply-all thread, a file-transfer link that expires before they've downloaded it, a shared-drive invite the client's IT blocks, and a 'can you just pull it off our website?'. They almost certainly have a form somewhere already — a Google Form, a free Typeform, a page on their Squarespace site — and each one failed in its own way: the client couldn't upload without signing into an account, or the packaged InDesign file was too big for the free tier, or the form itself carried someone else's logo at the bottom, which reads badly on the one document where they are selling their own taste in branding. They are not short of tooling and they are not technical; they are short of a single link they can paste into a kickoff email and trust. If the brief is thin, the first round of work is wrong, and the rework is unbilled.

segments.name: An indie SaaS founder or creator who keeps shipping features without knowing whether anyone asked for them
segments.situation: They are the product person, the support inbox and the release notes. Feedback reaches them as fragments: a Discord message, a churn email with no reason given, three support threads that turn out to be the same confusion. Bug reports arrive as 'it's broken on my end' with no screenshot and no browser, so every one costs a round trip. They have tried asking — an in-app link, a tweet, a survey emailed to their list — and the survey either died at a low response rate or hit a free-tier response cap partway through a run, which means the data they do have is a self-selected slice of their loudest users. Meanwhile the team, if there is a team, lives in Notion and Slack, and anything that lands in a separate dashboard nobody opens is effectively unread. The cost is not a number they track; it is a roadmap argued from anecdote and a quarter spent on the wrong thing.

segments.name: The ops or no-code person on a small team whose intake form is step one of an automation nobody owns
segments.situation: They inherited the form. It feeds something — a CRM record, a Slack channel, a billing step, an onboarding checklist — and the handoff between the form and the rest of the stack is currently a human. Someone exports a CSV on Mondays, or a scheduled job polls an API, or the form emails a shared inbox and a person retypes it. They have built the downstream half already in Make, Zapier or n8n and they are competent enough to read webhook docs, which means their evaluation is not about whether a form is pretty. It is about whether a delivery that fails at 2am gets retried, whether they will find out when it doesn't, whether they can verify a payload came from the vendor before it writes to a production database, and whether the vendor will move webhooks behind a seat-priced tier the quarter after they standardise on it. The failure they fear is specific and quiet: the form keeps accepting submissions and the records stop appearing.
segments.job_to_be_done: Make the handoff from 'someone filled in a form' to 'the system knows about it' stop depending on a person remembering

objections.objection: The free plan already does everything I need, so why would I ever pay — and if I never pay, you have no business asking me to.
objections.answer: This is self-inflicted and the honest answer is narrow: the vendor's own claim is that 99% of features are free (E111), so the paid upgrade is not 'more form builder'. Pro is for a specific short list — removing Tally's branding (E296), hosting on your own subdomain (E297), unlimited team members in shared workspaces (E298), workspaces and folders with access rights (E305), partial submissions (E299), drop-off analytics (E308), version history to 30 days (E309), and removing the 10 MB per-file ceiling (E306, E252). Cancel anytime (E242) makes it a per-project expense rather than a commitment. Nothing in the evidence quantifies the value of any of these, so copy that promises ROI here is unsupported.

objections.objection: Your own pages do not agree on what Pro costs. The pricing page says €20/month, the help pages say $29/month, and the comparison table prices custom domains at $29 and data retention at $89 while the plan page says Business is €65. If I cannot trust the price I cannot trust the plan.
objections.answer: Nothing in the supplied evidence resolves this. E270 (€20) and E271 (€65) come from the pricing page; E241 ($29/$290) and E259 ($89/$890) from the plan help pages; E68, E72, E76 and E102 repeat the dollar figures in the comparison material. There is no dated or canonical price in the ledger, so the conflict cannot be answered with what we know — it must be checked with the client before any email names a number.

objections.objection: 'Free forever' from a bootstrapped startup is a promise with a clock on it. You will get acquired, or raise prices, or decide my usage is no longer 'fair usage' — and by then my forms are embedded on client sites.
objections.answer: Partly answerable. They are independent, self-funded and bootstrapped with no outside investors (E20, E175, E178), have been going since 2020 (E19), are funded by customers rather than a runway, build in public with a public roadmap and documented milestones (E176, E177), and are at 500,000+ teams (E273, E320), which is the only durability signal in the ledger. The 'fair usage' half is not answered: the free offer is explicitly conditional on fair usage guidelines (E272, E328, E186) and the only ledger entry for the policy itself is a bare link (E160) with no stated thresholds. We cannot tell a reader where the line is.

objections.objection: I already have Google Forms in my Workspace and a Typeform the last person set up. Switching is a week of rebuilding forms that currently work, and re-embedding them everywhere they are embedded.
objections.answer: Partly answerable. Forms import in one click (E92), and the importer takes forms from other tools or even from a screenshot or PDF (E219); embedding works on WordPress, Webflow, Framer, Notion and any other site builder (E359, E220). On the 'why bother' half, the vendor's own comparison is the argument: respondents do not need to log in to upload files (E5), Google Forms has no custom domains (E71), no branding removal (E75), no formula editor (E59), no PDF export of submissions (E67), limited conditional logic (E55) and payments only via third parties (E63), while Typeform's free tier caps at 10 responses a month (E41) and charges for file uploads and payments (E49, E61). What the evidence does not cover: whether existing form URLs, embed snippets or historical responses survive a migration.

objections.answer: Answerable, but only on the paid tier: Pro hides all branding (E296, E243), hosts forms on your own subdomain for branded links (E297, E362, E244), lets you set the OG image, favicon, title and description so the link preview is yours (E304, E253), and allows custom CSS and built-in design control (E301, E300, E248). For borrowed credibility: 500,000+ teams including Notion, Make, Buy Me a Coffee, Rakuten and Glovo (E273, E274, E275, E276, E277, E278), Dribbble's Director of Advertising on choosing it for community surveys (E269), a Product Hunt Golden Kitty (E326), and press in Fast Company and The Brand Identity (E179, E180).

objections.objection: I cannot put candidate CVs, signed contracts or client data into a tool I have not vetted. Legal will ask where it is hosted, what the DPA says, and whether you have a security certification.
objections.answer: Strong on residency and weak on paperwork. Belgium-based EU company, GDPR compliant, all form data stored in Europe (E315, E376, E329, E97, E98, E330), encrypted in transit and at rest with stated control over what you collect (E316, E332), no cookie-tracking (E331), password protection and two-factor authentication on free plans (E99, E100, E207), reCAPTCHA (E204), and on Business automatic deletion of submissions after a set period for privacy compliance (E311, E261, E163, E317). What is missing from the evidence entirely: SOC 2 or ISO certification, a signable DPA, sub-processor list, or any audit. If the reader's blocker is procurement paperwork rather than hosting location, we cannot answer it.

objections.objection: We are a team, not a solo creator. Shared ownership, access control and someone overwriting a live form are my actual problems, and this looks like a tool for one person.
objections.answer: Answerable. Unlimited team members in shared workspaces (E298, E245, E155), forms grouped into workspaces and folders with managed team access rights (E305, E246), version history to restore a form 30 days back on Pro and 90 on Business (E309, E251, E313, E263), and webhook failures email both the form owner and the creator rather than one person (E27). Proof that teams at scale run on it: Notion, Make, Rakuten, Glovo (E274–E278), 500,000+ teams (E320), and the Make customer story on using a Tally form inside Customer Success (E264).

objections.objection: I could build this myself. A form page and an endpoint is an afternoon, and then I own it.
objections.answer: Answerable on the unglamorous half they are not costing in: delivery retries on a stated schedule — 5 minutes, 30 minutes, 1 hour, 6 hours, 1 day (E26); a one-time email to owner and creator when all retries fail, with the reason and a link to fix it (E27); SHA256 request signing via a Tally-Signature header so payloads can be verified before processing (E24, E34); a delivery event log with response inspection and manual retry (E35); unlimited webhook URLs with pause toggles (E25); a documented 10-second endpoint timeout (E23); and all of it free (E21). Plus the parts they would not build: 50+ languages and RTL (E358, E217), accessibility on semantic HTML with keyboard and screen-reader support on every plan (E93, E94, E95, E96), PDF generation per submission (E36, E218), and an MCP server and Claude connector (E30, E239, E222).

objections.objection: If it is genuinely unlimited and free, something must be worse — support, limits you have not published, or a product that stops being developed.
objections.answer: Partial. The vendor's framing is that 99% of features are free with no limits on forms, submissions or questions (E111, E183, E184), that there is no cap on number of files or total storage (E13) and no time limit on retention while the account is open (E14). Independent-ish signals: 4.8/5 user rating against 4.5 Typeform, 4.4 Jotform, 4.6 Google Forms (E88, E89, E90, E91), a Golden Kitty (E326), Sifted coverage of bootstrapping to multi-million ARR (E182), and a public roadmap with shipping documented publicly (E176, E177). Not answered: support response times or staffing, and the fair-usage thresholds (E160) that the whole free offer is conditioned on.

objections.objection: Not now. The form we have works well enough and this is not what my week is about.
objections.answer: The cheapest answer available: a form can be created with no signup at all (E319, E327, E380), existing forms import in one click (E92) or from a screenshot or PDF (E219), and Tally AI will generate or fix a form from plain language (E195), so the trial costs minutes rather than a project. Nothing in the evidence establishes a cost of waiting, so copy should not invent urgency here.
